6.0.0.en: "Chosen men": the elite, the choicest of the people.

6.0.1.en: David gathered thirty thousand of the choicest men of the people, leaders, wise men and elders, to share with him in moving the ark of the covenant to the city of David.

6.1.0.en: Baale of Judah: it is the same village of Kirjath-jearim mentioned in (1 Chr 13:6), a city on the border of Judah and Benjamin lying about 14 km west of Jerusalem. The ark was there since its removal from Beth-shemesh and remained until it was moved to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.

6.1.1.en: "That dwelleth between the cherubims": the cherubim are an angelic order that was beneath the throne of God (bearing the throne) when the Lord appeared to Ezekiel (Ezek 11:22), therefore He said to David, "that dwelleth between the cherubims."

6.1.2.en: They all went to where the ark was at that time, in "Baale of Judah," in the house of Abinadab, where the ark had remained since the children of Israel recovered it from the Philistines. It was placed for a short time in Beth-shemesh, then moved to the village of Kirjath-jearim (1 Sam 6). The ark remained in the village of Kirjath-jearim throughout the lifetime of Samuel and Saul and the beginning of David's reign while he was in Hebron, that is, about 75 years.

6.1.3.en: David's purpose in moving the ark was that it should be in the capital of the kingdom, which includes the king and the high priest, and because the ark was a symbol of the Lord's dwelling in the midst of His people. The ark was called by the name of the Lord of hosts, of whom it is said, "that dwelleth between the cherubims," because His glory was manifested between the two cherubim that were on the cover of the ark of the covenant. David also intended by moving the ark that the people be bound to God's presence in their midst.

6.2.0.en: Cart: a wagon drawn by animals, which here are oxen.

6.2.1.en: Abinadab: a man from the village of Kirjath-jearim who accepted that the ark of the covenant be in his house when it was sent back from the Philistines.

6.2.2.en: Gibeah: a high place in the village of Kirjath-jearim.

6.2.3.en: David and the priests of the Lord neglected the commandment concerning how the ark was to be carried when moved from one place to another, for it must be carried by the priests on their shoulders by the two staves assigned for carrying. Instead they set it on a new cart drawn by two oxen, which set out with it from the house of Abinadab, which was on a high place in the village of Kirjath-jearim, and "Uzzah and Ahio," the two sons or grandsons of Abinadab, were driving the oxen, and Ahio went in front leading the oxen while Uzzah walked behind the ark watching from behind.

6.3.0.en: Fir wood (cypress): a kind of wood distinguished by its durability and pleasant smell.

6.3.1.en: Harps (the oud): the plural of the oud, an instrument known since antiquity, known to many Eastern peoples and found depicted on Egyptian tombs, and still used today with some developments in it. It is a box with several strings, whose number ranges between 4 and 10 according to the type. David mastered playing it and its use spread among the children of Israel, and it was used in the rites of worship and on occasions of joy and feasts. Psalteries: a musical instrument in the shape of a triangle with four strings, played with the fingers. Timbrels: the plural of the tambourine, called in Egypt the "riqq." It consists of a membrane of animal skin stretched around a wooden frame in which small bells are fitted, and it makes a sound when struck.

6.3.2.en: Cornets (the harps): the plural of the harp, one of the ancient musical instruments.

6.3.3.en: Cymbals: they resemble the "cymbals" now used in our churches. They are two round plates of brass, which ring when one is struck against the other. The Hebrews used them in the rites of worship.

6.3.4.en: The procession of the ark was splendid, for David and the representatives of the people walked in the height of their happiness and joy, dancing and playing the musical instruments made of fir wood, among them harps, psalteries, timbrels, cornets and cymbals.

6.4.0.en: Nachon's threshingfloor: it is the same one called the threshingfloor of Chidon in (1 Chr 13:9). The threshingfloor is a level rocky ground on which they thresh grain to separate the chaff from it (a threshing floor). Nachon is the name of a person who owned a threshingfloor near Jerusalem.

6.4.1.en: "The oxen shook it": the oxen were unruly, that is, they stumbled and then rushed on quickly.

6.4.2.en: "The Lord had made a breach upon Uzzah": He struck him and put him to death.

6.4.3.en: It happened during the journey that the oxen suddenly became unruly, when they had reached the threshingfloor of Nachon in the middle of the road from Baale of Judah to Jerusalem. The oxen stumbled because of the roughness of the ground, and Uzzah feared that the ark would overturn and fall to the ground, so he put out his hand to steady the ark. This act aroused the anger of the Lord, and He put him to death at once.

6.4.4.en: God was not unjust in striking down Uzzah, because he was a Levite and knew that it is not right for anyone to touch the ark, but that it must be carried by the priests with two staves put through the rings of the ark. He must have understood this, because the ark was in his father's house, which had it for more than 70 years, so he had learned that no one may touch the ark. But it seems that he had become accustomed to the sight of the ark and its service, so he rushed without care lest it fall to the ground. It would have been better for Uzzah to insist on its being carried on the shoulders of the priests, and if priests were not available, then on the shoulders of the Levites, without anyone touching it.

6.4.5.en: We note that God permitted the cart drawn by the cows to go from the land of the Philistines to the lands of the children of Israel in peace, and the cattle did not become unruly. But here God permitted the oxen to become unruly, because the Jews know how the ark is to be carried by the priests. Sadly David forgot to consult God about how to move the ark, so what happened happened.

6.5.0.en: "Was displeased": he was affected by the death of Uzzah, who had taken care of the service of the ark for many years, but at the same time he was not objecting to God's command, because he knew that what happened was a carelessness on Uzzah's part in touching the ark. With the sudden death of Uzzah the joy of the people turned to sorrow, and David was distressed by the change of the situation and the clouding of the serenity of the occasion, and he called the place where Uzzah died "Perez-uzzah," that is, "the breach of Uzzah," because of his being put to death by the Lord. This name continued to be given to the place to the day of the writing of the book.

6.6.0.en: "Was afraid": he felt the awe and majesty of the ark to the point of trembling before it, because God is a mighty God and jealous for His holy things.

6.6.1.en: David realized that dealing with the ark requires complete precision in following what the Lord had legislated concerning it, because the Lord is a God jealous for His Law, and he, that is David, is a human being prone to error who might neglect to adhere to all that the presence of the ark in his city and under his possession requires, and he had seen the consequence of that before him in the Lord's putting Uzzah to death. Perhaps he wrote Psalm 15, "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle?" at that time.

6.7.0.en: David was afraid to move the ark to his city and asked a man named Obed-edom to keep the ark in his house. He was from the Philistine city of "Gath" and was living at that time on the road between the threshingfloor of Nachon and Jerusalem, and he was originally a Levite and was appointed afterwards to guard the ark (1 Chr 13:13). This shows the faith of Obed-edom, by which he surpassed David the prophet, for he accepted that the ark be in his house, and his faith overcame his fears, and he saw fit to adhere to the rites of reverence for the ark that the Law prescribes, trusting in God's blessing that he would receive.

6.7.1.en: The tender God is also the fearful and just One, so may you bow down before His sanctuary with reverence when you enter the church, then stand in your place and offer repentance and ask for His mercy and thank Him because He has granted you to enter His house, and He will reveal His secrets to you and give you joy in His presence with you, so that your heart rejoices in truth.

6.8.s.en: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

6.8.0.en: Obed-edom the Gittite: he was called the Gittite perhaps because he was from the town of Gath-rimmon, which was in the portion of Dan in the south and was given to the sons of Kohath (Josh 19:45, Josh 21:24), especially as Obed-edom was of the Korahites, descendants of Kohath (Num 16:1). The ark remained in the house of Obed-edom three months, and its presence in the house was a cause of blessing for him and for all his household. This was the natural reward for Obed-edom's faith, which distinguished him from the rest of the Jews, whose fear overshadowed their faith.

6.9.0.en: David learned of God's blessing upon the house of Obed-edom, so he went to him to take the ark from him, and commanded that a great procession be arranged to move it to his city Jerusalem, and everyone was glad to do this noble work. Here the humility of David appears, who learned from his previous mistake in leaving the ark in the house of Obed-edom out of fear of God, who punishes those who do not adhere to His Law, and he learned the humility of faith from Obed-edom, so he went to his house and asked him to take the ark to Jerusalem to be a blessing to the capital of the kingdom.

6.10.0.en: Whenever the bearers of the ark had gone six paces, for this time they carried the ark on the shoulders as the commandment requires, they would sacrifice an ox and a fatling, in atonement for their previous mistake in the way of carrying it, and as an expression of their thanks to the Lord and a celebration of the moving of the ark.

6.11.0.en: David was dancing with all enthusiasm in the procession of the ark, as an expression of his joy in the Lord and in the holy task he was performing, and he was wearing a linen garment, of the kind that the priests wore during the service and that those adhering to the Law wore on holy religious occasions. David took off his robe, which is the outer garment that represents grandeur, so the ephod, which represents purity, appeared, as he moved with joy and danced before the ark, declaring his humility and his joy at God's consenting to dwell in their midst and to live in the city of David to bless them, and showing his repentance for his neglect and shortcoming in not moving the ark quickly to his city Jerusalem. David sang Psalm 30 as an expression of his joy at the moving of the ark of God.

6.12.0.en: In their march, while carrying the ark, they used, in addition to the musical instruments mentioned before, trumpets and shouting as an expression of their great spiritual joy.

6.13.0.en: The procession reached the city of David, and the inhabitants of the city were looking out from the windows to watch the great procession. Michal, David's wife, also looked out from the window of her house and saw her husband the king leaping and dancing with joy. She did not like this conduct and considered it vulgar, lowering the dignity of the king and his majesty, for she believed in herself that the king must keep his dignity and grandeur at all times, therefore the king was lowered in her eyes. She was attached to the glories of the world and external grandeur.

6.13.1.en: Nothing of the grandeur of the procession caught Michal's attention except David's conduct. How much we also do like her when we criticize the conduct of others and their way of speaking or expression without caring about the content of what they say. So do not hasten to criticize, but look at the good conduct and good intention in people so that you benefit from everyone, and do not condemn the innocent as Michal did.

6.14.0.en: David had prepared a tent in his city to place the ark inside, so they set it in the midst of it.

6.14.1.en: This is different from the tabernacle of meeting, which at that time was in Gibeon (1 Chr 16:39). David and the people offered burnt offerings and peace offerings as an expression of their joy at the moving of the ark to the capital of the kingdom, and of their thanks to the Lord who permitted this work to be completed in peace. David wrote Psalm 30 at this time.

6.14.2.en: In (1 Chr 16:37-43) the inspired text mentions that Zadok the high priest and the rest of the priests remained in Gibeon to serve the tabernacle of meeting and offer the sacrifices, while the singers were appointed to serve the ark in Jerusalem. That is, the tabernacle of meeting with all its contents, the altar of brass, the altar of incense, the lampstand and the table of the showbread ... all this remained in Gibeon, and the ark alone was placed temporarily in a special tent in the city of David. The priest Abiathar served the ark in Jerusalem, and this arrangement continued until the days of Solomon, when Zadok alone became high priest, and he built a temple for the Lord and placed in it the ark and all the contents of the house of the Lord (1 Kgs 2:26, 27).

6.15.0.en: At the end of the assembly, after the offering of the sacrifices and burnt offerings, David prayed for the people and blessed them before sending them away, giving each one of them a loaf of bread, a cup of wine and a cake of dried figs as a sign of a fellowship of love among them. Bread, wine and figs were among the customary offerings to the Lord presented in His tent, and figs are among the trees that are widespread in the region. After that each one departed to his city, having taken part in the celebration of the return of the ark of the Lord into the midst of Jerusalem.

6.16.s.en: (3) Michal rebukes David for his dancing

6.16.0.en: Handmaids: the plural of handmaid, that is, a female servant.

6.16.1.en: After the great celebration ended, David also returned to bless his household as he had blessed the people. His wife Michal came out to meet him with disdain, reproaching him for the appearance in which he had shown himself before his people, without honor and without dignity, for he had taken off his robe and begun to leap and dance as the rabble of the people and the foolish among them do. In her contempt for David she said that his appearance was foolish before the maidservants who were looking from the windows and the servants who were on the road.

6.17.0.en: Her saying "How glorious was the king of Israel to day" means that his appearance was contemptible and foolish.

6.17.1.en: David was angered by her words and answered her that he was dancing and leaping before the Lord and not to put on a display before everyone, and that this dancing of his was only to express his joy in the Lord and his acknowledgment of His great work with him in choosing him as king for his people after rejecting her father Saul and his descendants. This dancing was like worship and joy for God and an honoring of Him, and not like the dancing of fools. The great God deserves this honor, and God chose him because he honors Him and submits to Him, whereas Saul God rejected because he was proud against Him. Thus he rebuked her for her lack of concern to honor God and her preoccupation with appearance and human grandeur, but there is no honor for any human being before God. This is the feeling of the humble David.

6.18.0.en: David said to her that before the Lord he feels his lowliness and the smallness of his rank, but among the servants he remains respected and glorified, for God exalts the humble and honors him and glorifies him before all his people.

6.19.0.en: Michal was barren and bore no children throughout her life, and perhaps this was a punishment, and barrenness was considered by the Jews a disgrace, because every woman hoped that the awaited Messiah would be born of her. The Holy Bible mentions in (2 Sam 21:8) that Michal had five children, but the truth is that they were the children of Merab her elder sister, who had died, and Michal adopted her five children and raised them, so they were ascribed to her, as Joseph was ascribed to Leah or to Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, as a mother, because Rachel had died (Gen 37:10).

6.19.1.en: To the degree that you humble yourself before God and before people, God exalts you in the sight of all and gives you grace and spiritual awe, so that people respect you and love you.

6.19.2.en: David's desire to build a house for the Lord and his prayer. The events of this chapter probably took place after chapter eight, that is, after David finished his wars, but it is mentioned here because it is connected with the moving of the ark mentioned in the previous chapter.
